title: Proper decision-tree learning in polynomial time
formal: Is there a uniform randomized membership-query algorithm that properly learns Boolean decision trees under the uniform distribution in polynomial time? For every \(n,s\geq1\), every integer \(m\geq2\), and every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a decision tree with at most \(s\) leaves, the learner is given \(n,s,m\) and oracle access to \(f\). It must output an explicitly represented decision tree \(h\), with probability at least \(2/3\), such that \[2^{-n}|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:h(x)\ne f(x)\}|\leq1/m.\] Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in \(n,s,m\).
why: The question tests whether efficient prediction can be achieved while retaining a decision-tree representation in a basic, well-specified query model. Its resolution would clarify the computational cost of proper learning beyond sample complexity alone.
status_note: The exact uniform-distribution proper query question is explicit in the 2022 source. Checked later hardness results do not cover this distributional setting. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no polynomial-time learner or unconditional impossibility theorem for the stated model.

progress.text: The open-problem paper records an almost-polynomial proper learner and asks for a polynomial bound.
Distribution-free proper query learning is shown NP-hard; this does not settle the uniform case.
New connections to nearest-codeword approximation give further learning hardness under different distributional/access assumptions.

importance.reason: A central proper-learning question, with a near-polynomial algorithm but no polynomial bound for the uniform membership-query setting; representation and access to labels both materially affect its complexity.

sentences: Proper learning of decision trees requires the learner to output a decision tree, preserving the target representation's simple branching structure.
The source asks for a polynomial-time algorithm under the uniform input distribution with membership queries available.
Those queries let the learner choose inputs and observe their target labels, making this different from learning from random examples alone.
Existing algorithms in the source are faster than earlier quasipolynomial approaches but still fall short of polynomial time.
A solution would provide an efficient way to recover an interpretable tree hypothesis without abandoning the tree representation during learning.

source_formulation.text: Design a \(\operatorname{poly}(n, s, 1/\varepsilon )\)-time membership query algorithm for properly learning size-s decision trees over n variables to error \(\varepsilon\) under the uniform distribution.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

source_consolidations.reason: Same proper membership-query decision-tree learning target under the uniform distribution. Precise source wording retained here.

definitions: A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node queries one coordinate \(x_i\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its two outgoing edges correspond to values zero and one. Leaves are labelled zero or one; following the input’s path defines the output bit. Size means the number of leaves. Repeated coordinate tests are allowed. The unknown target need only admit a tree with at most \(s\) leaves; that tree is not supplied. A membership query may be any chosen bit string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and returns the exact noiseless bit \(f(x)\). The learner is one finite probabilistic multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice, and no other oracle. Writing the \(n\)-bit query costs ordinary bit steps; reading its returned label costs one. All random-bit generation, computation and output are charged. Its time is bounded by \(K(n+s+m+1)^a\) on every target and every random execution, for constants \(K,a\) independent of parameters. Integers are supplied in binary. The accuracy convention \(\varepsilon=1/m\) specifies the usual inverse-accuracy parameter without an arbitrary real input encoding; existence for these accuracies is equivalent to existence for arbitrary requested positive accuracy by rounding to a smaller reciprocal accuracy. Properness is weak properness: the output must be a decision tree, but need not have at most \(s\) leaves. Its full explicit description, with variable indices, children and leaf bits, must fit the polynomial time bound. The success probability concerns the learner’s randomness; prediction error is measured over a fresh uniform point and the guarantee holds for every promised target.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that a learner satisfying all these quantifiers exists, or that no such learner exists. The positive direction requires polynomial bit time, a proper explicit tree output and the uniform-distribution error bound with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative result must rule out all randomized learners of this kind, including those allowed polynomial-size trees larger than the target. An improper hypothesis, a random-examples-only result, distribution-free hardness alone, or a conditional obstruction whose assumption is unproved does not settle the stated existence question.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 1 asks for polynomial time in the number of variables, target size and inverse accuracy. The source explicitly distinguishes strict properness, which preserves the target size bound, from weak properness, which merely returns a tree; its question is open even for the latter.

The representation constraint matters: an efficient predictor need not come with a comparably small tree representation. Membership queries also matter because they let the learner choose inputs instead of relying only on the examples that a distribution happens to provide.

The source’s Theorem 2 reports an almost-polynomial proper query learner, with time \(\widetilde O(n^2)(s/\varepsilon)^{O(\log((\log s)/\varepsilon))}\). In the usual polynomial-size, constant-error regime this yields \(n^{O(\log\log n)}\), which still exceeds a fixed polynomial.

Koch, Strassle and Tan prove NP-hardness for distribution-free proper learning with queries in FOCS 2023. Their paper explicitly contrasts that result with the easier uniform-distribution setting. A lower bound obtained from a specially chosen distribution does not rule out this card’s learner.

Their FOCS 2024 coding-theoretic work gives further hardness connections for decision-tree learning. Its discussion distinguishes the remaining uniform-distribution problem from the distributions used in its reductions.

An empirical tree-fitting procedure and its success on a finite collection of datasets are not the universal learning guarantee. The error bound must hold for every small-tree target, even when the target’s structure is unknown and the output tree has a different topology.
